### **I. The First Spark**

The village of Eldermere had always been a quiet place. Its cobblestone streets, lined with willow trees that bent low over the river, carried the scent of damp earth and the faintest hint of pine from the distant woods. The people here lived simple lives—farming the fertile soil, weaving wool into blankets, and telling stories by firelight of the time when the woods were not just a boundary, but a living thing.

But no one spoke of the woods like that anymore.

Not since the last child who wandered too far had returned with hollow eyes and a voice that slithered like a snake. Not since the old woman in the market square had whispered that the trees remembered everything—names, secrets, the way a child’s laughter had once echoed through the undergrowth before it was silenced forever.

Lena had never been one to listen to such warnings. While the others in her village stayed close to the hearth, she wandered the edges of the woods, drawn by something deeper than curiosity. She had seen things there—glimpses of light that didn’t belong to the sun, shadows that moved when no one was looking, the way the air seemed to hum when the wind carried voices from beyond the trees.

One evening, as the sun bled into the horizon, she found herself at the edge of the Blackthorn Grove, where the trees grew twisted and gnarled, their bark etched with symbols no one could decipher. The air was thick with the scent of damp moss and something older, something like decay and something like life.

She knelt, pressing her palm against the bark of an ancient oak. The wood was warm beneath her touch, as if it had known her long before she knew herself.

*"You’re here,"* a voice murmured.

Lena jerked back, her breath catching. The voice wasn’t coming from the tree—it was coming from *inside* her head, a whisper that slithered into her mind like smoke.

She had heard it before. In her dreams. In the way the wind carried whispers when the village elders spoke of the woods.

*"You’re not afraid,"* the voice continued. *"That’s why I chose you."*

Lena’s heart pounded. She had heard stories of the *Hollowborn*—entities that dwelled in the deepest parts of the woods, creatures born from forgotten magic, from the things that had been buried too long. They fed on curiosity, on the hunger to know what lay beyond the veil of the ordinary.

She stood, her fingers trembling. "Who are you?"

The voice laughed, a sound like rustling leaves. *"I am the one who listens. I am the one who remembers. And you, Lena, are the first to ask."*

### **II. The Offer**

The next morning, Lena returned to the grove alone. The trees seemed to lean in, their branches forming a canopy that blocked out the sun. She pressed her ear to the bark again, and this time, the whisper was louder, clearer.

*"You want to know what the woods remember,"* it said. *"Then you must bring me something in return."*

Lena’s stomach twisted. "What?"

*"A memory,"* the voice replied. *"One that has been buried too deep. One that you have forgotten."*

She had no memories like that. Not the kind that could be taken. But then, she thought of the night before, of the way the trees had seemed to *watch* her. Of the way her reflection in the river had moved when she wasn’t looking.

She had seen things. She had *felt* things.

*"I don’t know what you want,"* she lied. *"But I’ll do anything."*

The whispering grew louder, more insistent. *"Then bring me the thing that makes you afraid."*

Lena’s breath hitched. She had never been afraid of the woods. Not really. But there was something in the way the trees had moved, in the way the air had shifted when she wasn’t looking. She had seen her own shadow twist, as if it were alive.

She reached into her pocket and pulled out the small, silver locket she had given to her younger brother, Elias, before he vanished into the woods one winter night. The locket was empty now, its contents long since lost to the cold. But it was the only thing she had that could be taken.

She held it out to the trees.

The whispering stopped.

Then, the trees *moved*.

The branches parted like a curtain, revealing a path that had never been there before—a winding trail of moss and twigs, leading deeper into the heart of the grove. Lena followed it, her heart pounding, her mind racing.

At the end of the path stood a figure.

It was not human. Not entirely. Its form was shifting, like smoke given shape, its limbs too long, its eyes too many—dozens of them, like the facets of a gemstone, reflecting the light in ways that made her head spin.

*"You have given me what I asked,"* the Hollowborn said. *"Now, you must give me what I remember."*

Lena’s hands trembled. She had no idea what she was doing. But she had to know. She had to understand.

She stepped forward.

### **III. The Price of Knowledge**

The Hollowborn did not speak again. It did not move. It simply *waited*, its many eyes fixed on her.

Lena closed her eyes. She thought of the night Elias had vanished. Of the way the wind had carried his voice, whispering secrets she couldn’t understand. Of the way the trees had seemed to *watch* him, as if they had known him before he knew himself.

She thought of the way she had seen her own reflection move when she wasn’t looking. Of the way the river had seemed to laugh when she had thrown a stone into its surface.

And then, she thought of the way she had felt—*seen*—when she had pressed her palm against the oak. Not just a feeling, but a *remembering*. A memory that had been buried for centuries, waiting to be unearthed.

She opened her eyes.

The Hollowborn’s form rippled, like water disturbed by a stone. Then, it *spoke*, not in words, but in images.

She saw Elias’s face, not as she remembered it, but as he had been when he was young—before the woods had claimed him. She saw the way his hair had been, the way his eyes had shone when he laughed. She saw the moment he had looked at her, and she had known, without a doubt, that he was hers.

She saw the river, not as it was now, but as it had been when the Hollowborn had first taken shape. She saw the way the water had flowed, not just over the land, but *through* it, carrying secrets that had been buried for ages.

And then, she saw herself.

Not as she was now, but as she had been when she was a child, before the woods had whispered to her. She saw the way she had run through the fields, the way she had laughed at the sky. She saw the moment she had looked into the river and seen her own reflection move, as if it were alive.

The Hollowborn’s form shimmered. *"You have given me what I remember,"* it said. *"Now, you must give me what I am."*

Lena’s breath caught. She had no idea what it meant. But she knew, deep in her bones, that she had done something terrible.

The Hollowborn reached out, its many fingers brushing against her skin. She screamed, but the sound was swallowed by the wind, by the whispering of the trees.

Then, the world went dark.

When Lena woke, she was not in the grove. She was in a room that was not a room at all, but a space between worlds—a place where the air was thick with the scent of damp earth and something older, something like the woods themselves.

She was not alone.

There were others like her. Girls, like her, with hollow eyes and voices that slithered like snakes. They sat in a circle, their fingers tracing patterns in the air, their lips moving in silent song.

*"You are not alone,"* one of them said. *"We are all the Hollowborn."*

Lena’s hands trembled. She had heard stories of the Hollowborn, of the way they fed on memories, on the things that had been buried too deep. But she had never believed them.

Now, she knew.

She had become one of them.

The Hollowborn did not let her go. It did not let her leave the grove. It did not let her forget what she had done.

Instead, it made her a part of it. It made her a part of the woods. It made her a part of the Hollowborn.

She learned to move through the trees like a shadow, to hear the whispers of the wind like a song. She learned to see the world in a way that no one else could—she saw the things that were hidden, the things that were forgotten.

But she also learned the cost of her curiosity.

The Hollowborn fed on memories, on the things that had been buried too deep. It fed on the things that had been lost, the things that had been forgotten. And it fed on the things that had been taken from the world.

Lena saw the way the villagers looked at her now. She saw the way they avoided her, as if she were something unclean. She saw the way they whispered about the woods, about the way the trees had taken something from her.

She saw the way the river had changed. It no longer flowed as it had before. It no longer carried the same secrets. It carried the weight of the Hollowborn, of the things that had been buried too deep.

She saw the way the world had changed.

And she saw the way she had changed.

She was not the same girl who had wandered into the woods. She was not the same girl who had asked questions. She was not the same girl who had forgotten what she had done.

She was the Hollowborn.
